audience: New applicants need to assemble supporting documents and recognize youth-specific consent and school requirements.
accuracy: Document categories are described as handbook examples, not a promise that any particular applicant’s documents will be accepted. The county office and ITD decide acceptability.
dynamic: Current document acceptance lists and links, donor contribution amounts and service contacts need an official refresh before use as live application guidance.
mis: A secondary identity document by itself does not establish identity; a supporting document must accompany the primary proof.
mnemonic: Identity, address and consent is a teaching checklist for assembling the application evidence.
glossary: Lawful presence concerns eligibility to be in the country; a liability signer accepts legal responsibility; VOC records school compliance.
skills: Distinguish regular and Star Card documentation
debts: The checklist on physical page twenty-one lists proof of citizenship alongside lawful-presence documents; preserve the noncitizen eligibility rules on later pages rather than treating citizenship as universally mandatory.
C: Idaho treats a person who has never held a license in any jurisdiction as a new applicant.
A person returning to Idaho after obtaining a credential elsewhere is considered a new applicant.
A person surrendering another jurisdiction’s license is treated as a new applicant.
An Idaho license that expired twenty-five months or more earlier puts the holder in the new-applicant category.
A new credential application requires evidence of age and identity.
A new credential application requires verification of a Social Security card or number.
A new credential application requires evidence of Idaho residency.
Where applicable, a new credential application requires lawful-presence documents.
A new applicant may need visual or medical certification when it applies to the applicant.
Applicants younger than seventeen must provide driver training completion evidence.
Applicants younger than eighteen need a liability signer.
Applicants younger than eighteen must supply school-compliance verification.
The county office must verify age and identity before issuing a license or identification card.
Surrendering a state photo credential together with a United States birth certificate showing the full legal name and birth date is sufficient age-and-identity evidence.
The age-and-identity documents described in the handbook cannot be submitted as photocopies or faxes.
A driver privilege card does not qualify as age-and-identity evidence.
An other-state license or identification card needs a United States birth certificate or equivalent to serve as identity evidence in Idaho.
An applicant younger than eighteen does not have to possess a photo identification card.
A minor without photo identification may use a parent’s or guardian’s photo identification with the child’s certified original birth certificate and any necessary guardianship evidence.
When a minor presents an accepted photo identification document, extra parental or guardian identification is unnecessary.
A birth certificate submitted for identity proof must be accompanied by an accepted photo identity document.
When a birth certificate name differs from the current name, a secondary document must connect the names.
A certified marriage certificate or court name-change document can connect a birth name with the current legal name.
An Idaho photo license or identification card expired less than five years is listed as acceptable photo identity evidence.
An other-state photo license or identification card expired less than five years is listed as acceptable photo identity evidence.
An acceptable valid Homeland Security photo document is listed as photo identity evidence.
Military identification, including retired or dependent military cards, appears among the accepted photo identity documents.
A valid United States passport or passport card is listed as acceptable photo identity evidence.
An original citizenship or naturalization document is listed among photo identity documents.
A foreign passport is listed among the accepted identity documents.
An Idaho concealed-weapons permit expired no more than one year is listed among the photo identity documents.
A veteran Universal Access Card carrying a photograph is listed as photo identity evidence.
A Native American identification card with a photograph is listed as photo identity evidence.
A Transportation Workers Identity Credential is listed as photo identity evidence.
A junior or senior high school photo card is listed as acceptable photo identity evidence, but a college or university photo card is excluded from that example.
A junior high, senior high, college, university or military annual yearbook is listed among identity evidence.
Photo identification from Idaho Corrections or Juvenile Corrections is listed among the accepted identity documents.
C2: A foreign national may substitute a foreign passport for the certified United States birth certificate.
For a foreign national’s identity, the handbook requires a valid foreign passport and acceptable lawful-presence evidence.
Secondary identity documents cannot establish identity on their own.
A secondary identity document must show the name and enough information to support part or all of the primary identity evidence.
A certified court name-change record is listed as a secondary identity document.
A certified marriage record meeting Idaho standards needs the seal and recorded document number to serve as the listed secondary evidence.
A certified divorce record from a court or state vital-records office is listed as secondary identity evidence.
Guardianship or custody records must be notarized or court-certified to qualify as the listed secondary evidence.
Military discharge papers are listed as secondary identity evidence.
Every submitted document must be acceptable to both ITD and the county driver’s license office.
The Social Security Administration’s online verification system must verify the applicant’s Social Security number.
An Idaho license or identification card does not display the holder’s Social Security number.
An applicant must live within Idaho to receive an Idaho license or identification card.
Residency evidence must show a physical address and may include a lease, utility bill, employment record or school-enrollment record.
The documents used as Idaho residency evidence must be dated within one year.
A person without lawful presence in the United States is ineligible for an Idaho license or identification card.
An issuance or renewal may require lawful-presence evidence when citizenship proof was never provided or ITD has no record of it.

Listed lawful-presence evidence includes an original certified United States birth certificate, a valid United States passport, a birth-abroad certificate or an original naturalization or citizenship certificate.
A permanent resident card, resident-alien card or employment authorization card is listed among lawful-presence evidence.
A valid foreign passport together with the arrival-departure record is listed among lawful-presence evidence.
For someone who is neither a citizen nor permanent legal resident, license validity ends at the documented lawful-stay end date or after four years, whichever comes first.
When Homeland Security documents have no expiration date, the license for a noncitizen who is not a permanent legal resident expires one year after issuance.
A visual or medical condition affecting driving may require a physician’s statement that the applicant can drive safely.
After eye surgery improves vision, a physician’s note may support removal of a license restriction.
An applicant younger than seventeen must document both approved driver training completion and completion of supervised instruction requirements.
A license applicant younger than eighteen needs a parent or legal guardian to consent and assume legal responsibility for the applicant’s driving.
A liability signer other than a birth-certificate parent must document legal authority to consent.
The liability signer’s identity must be verified.
A signer whose name differs from the birth-certificate name may need additional documents establishing the relationship.
An absent liability signer must give another person signing authority through a power-of-attorney form.
Before the applicant turns eighteen, the liability signer can withdraw consent at any time and the department will cancel the driving credential.
A married applicant’s spouse may act as liability signer if the spouse is at least eighteen.
An applicant younger than eighteen must show acceptable evidence of attendance and enrollment in, or graduation from, a recognized high school or equivalent program.
A compliance slip, high school diploma or general-education completion certificate may document school compliance.
The parent or guardian signing liability consent must also affirm compliance with Idaho’s school-attendance provisions.
A Star Card application needs identity, photograph and lawful-presence evidence.
A Star Card applicant needs name-change evidence when the legal name has changed.
A Star Card applicant’s Social Security number is verified with the Social Security Administration.
A Star Card application requires two proofs showing an Idaho physical residence address.
The donor designation may be requested beginning at age fifteen.
A donor designation communicates the holder’s wish to donate organs or tissue after death.
A donor applicant younger than eighteen needs consent from a parent or adult guardian.
For a veteran designation, the handbook lists military discharge documentation indicating honorable discharge.
